## TL;DR

I closed the responsive QA evidence gap for task creation and editing. The fixture suite now drives actual controls in the production `TaskDrawer` at 375 px, 768 px, and 1280 px, including dependency selection, priority, area, screenshot selection, and task save/patch calls. A headless WebKit test measures the production drawer markup with its compiled styles. I revised the QA record to distinguish interaction coverage from browser geometry evidence.

## Work and rationale

The automated review identified a mismatch between the QA document and what the earlier tests proved. Setting `window.innerWidth` in jsdom did not measure layout. Emitting area or priority changes directly skipped the controls. Pushing a screenshot fixture into Pinia skipped the file picker path. The standalone overflow fixture used a handcrafted form and copied CSS, so it was not evidence about the production drawer.

I kept the interaction tests at the component level because they can efficiently repeat real control use at all three widths while stubbing only repository writes. The create test opens the new task drawer, selects its manual form, fills the title, chooses an area and priority from the rendered pickers, selects a prerequisite, and passes a PNG through the actual screenshot input. It then verifies the create payload and that the screenshot upload receives the created task ID. The edit case changes the same relevant fields through the form controls and checks the patch payload. Prerequisite selection and removal is also covered in the picker interaction case.

Component tests still cannot establish physical pixel geometry. For that, I added a headless WebKit test that mounts the actual `TaskDrawer` to produce markup, then loads the Vite compiled global CSS and Vue compiled scoped stylesheet alongside that markup. It checks the drawer bounds, overflow, and the bounds of visible controls at the requested widths. This removes the copied form/CSS from the previous check and makes geometry assertions about the production component’s rendered structure and styles. I rewrote the QA document to describe these two forms of evidence separately and to state the remaining limits plainly.

I also removed the obsolete handcrafted overflow fixture. It no longer represents the coverage we want, and retaining it would invite reviewers to mistake its copied picker styling for actual drawer verification.

## Approaches tried

I first tried to mount the whole Vue component directly in the WebKit page by asking Vite to serve its browser module graph. That graph imports server-oriented modules which depend on Node built-ins, so it cannot run as a standalone browser page without building a different application entry point. I then used the actual component’s JSDOM-rendered markup, attached the actual compiled styles, and measured that in WebKit. This kept the browser test focused on layout while the component suite remained responsible for interactions.

The screenshot path initially failed because FileReader completes asynchronously in jsdom. I added a deterministic test FileReader fixture and wait for its callback-driven store update. The fixture still enters through the actual `<input type="file">` change handler and the production dropzone’s emitted file list; only image decoding is deterministic.

## Challenges and blockers

One earlier WebKit assertion selected the outer Radix dialog wrapper rather than the drawer’s `.drawer-wrap`, so it measured the wrong box. I changed the locator to the actual drawer shell. I also had to extract the CSS string from Vite’s generated module safely because it contains escaped quotes and multiline CSS. The component scope ID comes from Vite’s transformed `TaskDrawer` module and is passed to Vue’s style compiler so scoped rules match the captured markup. The measurement disables animations and transitions so it records the stable open state instead of an intermediate slide position. The route fixture includes both destinations used by the drawer so router warnings do not obscure test output.

The first browser geometry runs found that the panel’s slide-in animation was still moving the drawer when bounds were sampled. Disabling animation in the measurement document made the check deterministic and verifies the stable final layout. After that change, WebKit measured the actual drawer successfully at all three widths. No external account, live service, or physical device was required for this fixture based scope.

## Key learnings

Viewport values in a DOM simulator are inputs to responsive logic, not evidence that CSS geometry works. A strong responsive check should separate stateful interaction assertions from browser measurements and use the same component markup and styles shipped to users. The WebKit check makes stable layout claims only: interactions are covered in the component suite, where events and resulting repository payloads can be asserted directly.

Testing a screenshot upload path should begin at the user-facing file input, then wait for the asynchronous reader before checking the queued attachment. A deterministic reader fixture removes image decoding as a source of timing variance while preserving the actual input change handler and emitted file list. Finally, QA notes should name these boundaries so later readers do not infer live upload or device coverage from mocked fixtures.
